title: "Non-exponential infectious periods"

## The assumption in $-\gamma I$

- A constant recovery hazard makes the infectious period **exponential**.
- Exponential is *memoryless*: infected three weeks ago is no more likely to
  recover tomorrow than infected yesterday.
- Its mode is at **zero** and its coefficient of variation is exactly **1**.

Real infections have a typical duration. Fixing this changes the epidemic far
more than most people expect.

::: {.notes}
Students accept -γI without noticing what it implies about individuals. Survival
is exp(-γa), so the single most likely outcome is to recover almost immediately.
Say that out loud; it usually lands.
:::

## One assumption, six implementations

| Distribution | Technique | Base model |
|---|---|---|
| Exponential | constant hazard | everything so far |
| Erlang | method of stages | ODE |
| Fixed | delay equation | DDE |
| Fixed + noise | stochastic delay equation | SDDE |
| Fixed, individual | scheduled recovery | jump process |
| Arbitrary | age of infection | PDE |

::: {.notes}
The biology is identical throughout: same R0, same mean period. Only the shape
of the distribution changes. Organising by technique rather than by disease is
what makes the comparison possible.
:::

## Method of stages

$n$ infectious compartments in series, each left at rate $n\gamma$:

$$
\dot I_j = n\gamma\,(I_{j-1} - I_j)
$$

- Total period is $\operatorname{Erlang}(n, n\gamma)$.
- Mean stays $1/\gamma$; **CV becomes $1/\sqrt{n}$**.
- $n=1$ is the ordinary SIR model; $n\to\infty$ approaches a fixed period.

::: {.notes}
This is the linear chain trick. The appeal is that nothing leaves ODE tooling —
no delays, no history, just more compartments. The cost is that only integer
Erlang shapes are reachable.
:::

## Same mean, same $R_0$, different epidemic

| Stages $n$ | CV | Peak $I$ | Peak time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (exponential) | 1.00 | 158 | 17.5 |
| 2 | 0.71 | 209 | 14.5 |
| 5 | 0.45 | 259 | 12.5 |
| 20 | 0.22 | 296 | 12.0 |
| ∞ (fixed delay) | 0 | **351** | 11.0 |

The peak **more than doubles**, purely from distributional shape.

::: {.notes}
This table is the chapter. Emphasise that R0 = 2 and the mean period is 4 in
every row. Anyone who has ever converted a growth rate into R0 has implicitly
assumed a generation-interval distribution, and this is the size of that
assumption.
:::

## Why: the generation interval

- Exponential period puts a large share of transmission in a **long tail**.
- A fixed period delivers the same transmission in a **narrow window**.
- Shorter generation interval ⟹ faster growth at the *same* $R_0$.

So the epidemic arrives earlier and higher, without anyone becoming more
infectious.

::: {.notes}
The key point for interpretation: R0 alone does not determine the epidemic curve.
Growth rate and R0 are linked through the generation-interval distribution, and
assuming exponential is not the conservative choice.
:::

## Fixed delay: a delay equation

$$
\dot I(t) = \beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N - \beta c\,S(t-\tau)I(t-\tau)/N
$$

- Those recovering now are exactly those infected $\tau$ ago.
- The state is a **history** on $[t-\tau, t]$, not a point.
- Needs an initial *function*, and `constant_lags` so the solver places a step at
  the discontinuity.

::: {.notes}
Warn about the discontinuity at t = τ: it propagates, and adaptive solvers can
step over it and silently lose accuracy. With noise added, in a stochastic delay
equation, adaptivity around it becomes unreliable and a fixed step is safer.
:::

## Individuals: schedule the recovery

- When someone is infected, put their recovery time in a queue.
- Handles **any** distribution, exactly, at the individual level.
- But the process is **non-Markovian**: the next event depends on history, so the
  plain direct method no longer applies.

::: {.notes}
This is the most flexible route and the one closest to how you would simulate a
real cohort. The cost is bookkeeping: a queue alongside the infection hazard.
:::

## Takeaways

- A constant recovery rate is a **modelling choice**, not a neutral default.
- Stages give Erlang cheaply; delays give fixed periods exactly; scheduling gives
  anything, individually; the age-of-infection PDE gives anything, in aggregate.
- Holding $R_0$ fixed, distributional shape moves the peak by a factor of two.
- Check what your generation-interval assumption is doing before trusting a
  growth-rate conversion.

::: {.notes}
Point at the age-structure chapter for the PDE machinery, and note that the same
McKendrick equation underlies both, read with a as infection age rather than
chronological age.
:::
